Just because you book meetings with cold email doesn't mean you will with LinkedIn DMs or cold calls.

What books a meeting on email, LinkedIn and the phone are three different things. Each one needs its own playbook.

1/ Cold email, your volume engine. 20 to 25 sends a day from each warmed inbox.

About half the companies that come to us arrive with their sending domains already burned, so start with the domains.

→ Your main domain never sends cold email. Buy "get" versions of your domain and put 3 inboxes on each.
→ SPF, DKIM and DMARC on every one, then 2 to 4 weeks of warm-up before the first send. Leave it on after launch.
→ Bounces above 2% damage the domain. So does mail that fails any of the 3 records.
→ Send on a signal. Clay's new hire and funding alerts move a strong-fit account up to Tier 1, and email 1 opens on the latest one.
→ Instantly's average sender gets 3.43% replies. Our signal campaigns run 5 to 18%.

We build the list in Clay with Prospeo and send from Instantly or lemlist.

2/ LinkedIn DMs, your precision play. Don't judge this one on replies.

In one platform's 257K sends I saw AI-personalized messages get more replies and fewer meetings, 0.93 per 100 sends against 1.02. Count meetings.

→ Save the 2 or 3 buyers at each Tier 1 and Tier 2 account to a Sales Navigator lead list.
→ Every morning, check who viewed your profile, who liked or commented and who followed the company page. Send the request right after and say so in the note.
→ Message 1 goes the day after they accept. Lead with something useful, ask for the call in the next one.
→ Withdraw anything older than 3 weeks. LinkedIn restricts your invites when too many sit pending.
→ Reachium's 180,155 requests: 27.1% accepted, 2% of those booked.

lemlist runs the visit, the request and both messages as one sequence. Profile viewers and new followers we still add by hand.

3/ Cold calling, your Tier 1 closer. Belkins logged 175,000+ dials and booked about 1 meeting per 370.

Our own ran about 1 per 37, and even that only paid for itself on seven-figure deals, so we cut the phone for everything under Tier 1.

→ Check the do-not-call rules for every country on the list before you buy any mobiles.
→ Pull Tier 1 mobiles with Prospeo, scrub them against the registry, load them into Nooks. It dials several numbers at once and hands your rep whoever picks up.
→ Call the day after email 1 and open on the same situation. Keep the calendar open so the invite goes out before you hang up.
→ No answer? Leave a voicemail that points to the email. In Gong's data that took email replies from 2.73% to 5.87%. Stop at 2.
→ Log every dial as a conversation, a pickup, a voicemail or no answer, so you know your own numbers.
→ Skip generic title lists. Those people get dialed all day and stopped picking up a long time ago.

So tier the list first, and give each tier its own channels:

→ Tier 1, strong fit with an active signal: a call, LinkedIn and email, one custom message per account.
→ Tier 2, strong fit, no signal yet: LinkedIn and email, from a template with one variable swapped.
→ Everyone else: email only, in high-volume sequences.

Push a Tier 1 account into a high-volume email sequence and you burn it.

The 3 emails, the connection note and the voicemail are in the article (bookmark it for later).

I'm begging you:

- open Claude Code and give it one folder to work from before you connect any tools
- put the standing rules in CLAUDE.md: who you sell to, what tone to write in, what never to say. Keep it under 200 lines, past that it starts dropping rules
- put the GTM substance in brain.md: your ICP, your best angles, your 3 best closed deals
- rank your sources at the bottom of that file, closed-won CRM data first, so the model stops picking a winner silently
- connect each data tool with one claude mcp add line, and single-quote the key or it ends up in the file you're about to commit
- dictate the campaign in 3 sentences. Louis on our team did exactly that and had a verified list and the copy sitting in Instantly 27 minutes later
- let it tier the accounts: T1 fits and has a live signal, T2 fits with nothing live yet, T3 goes on a watchlist
- enrich emails for everyone and phones for T1 only, a phone lookup costs about 10x an email
- write one prompt per T1 account off its signal, one template with a variable swapped for T2, the volume sequence for T3
- send it to 500 prospects instead of 100,000. Micro-lists get 20-30% replies, blasts get 2-3%, across 1M+ emails we analyzed in Instantly
- read every T1 email yourself before anything goes out, that's the only part still yours

2114725336852132160.text:
🦔Anthropic’s full IPO filing is out, and it plans to list on Nasdaq as ANT. Revenue hit $16.3 billion in the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion a year earlier, and the business brought in $3.9 billion more cash than it spent running itself. The $80.7 billion headline loss is almost entirely accounting on its convertible notes, which turn into stock at the IPO.

My Take
Anthropic grew fast, and a lot of that growth runs on money from the companies selling it chips and cloud capacity. It has raised $141 billion so far, and Google, Amazon and Broadcom have another $77 billion lined up, mostly tied to Anthropic using more of their compute. Even the positive cash flow came partly from paying those suppliers later. Suppliers lending a customer the money to keep buying from them is the same setup Nvidia runs with CoreWeave.

And most of the revenue comes from usage instead of long contracts. About 80% is pay-as-you-go, and the filing admits many top customers can cut spending at any time. This half also lined up with companies pushing staff to rack up AI usage, right before corporate budget reviews. (Earlier reporting on the draft put compute commitments at $518 billion or more. The public filing leaves that number blank.) Public buyers barely get a vote. The founders keep 50.1% and a trust picks most of the board. I expect a hot first day and a much harder 2027, once finance teams review their AI budgets and usage growth slows.

SpaceX $SPCX has signed a binding commitment letter with an Apollo Global Management-managed entity for a massive $40B GPU financing arrangement to support its expanding AI data center infrastructure. The transaction is expected to close before year-end, with GPU deliveries and lease payments beginning in the first half of 2027. Despite the growth, Anthropic reported an $80.7B net loss, largely driven by a $72.4B noncash fair-value charge tied to convertible notes, while its operating loss narrowed to $693M. The biggest revelation is the company's enormous AI infrastructure commitments extending as far as 2045, including approximately $161B in Broadcom TPU leases, $120.5B with SpaceXAI, $114.5B with Google, $110B with Amazon, $44.9B with Microsoft, and tens of billions more with Nscale, Lambda, and AMD, alongside roughly $245B in additional agreements signed after June 30. Levy noted that much of the recent discussion surrounding Tesla has focused on a potential merger with SpaceX $SPCX, which he believes could result in a premium for Tesla shareholders. However, his bullish thesis extends beyond a possible combination, citing improving automotive demand, strong growth in Tesla's energy business, and a sharp acceleration in Robotaxi miles driven. Barclays also highlighted FSD adoption exceeding 75% of new North American vehicle deliveries, suggesting growing monetization opportunities for Tesla's autonomous driving technology. Together, these factors underpin the firm's more constructive outlook on Tesla's long-term growth potential.

The program reportedly covers select teams across the United States, Canada, United Kingdom, and India, with eligible employees receiving severance packages in exchange for voluntarily leaving the company. Employees have until early December to decide whether to participate, with departures expected to take place by year-end. The move could represent one of Microsoft's largest workforce restructuring initiatives, although the final number of departures will depend on employee participation.

5. Samsung and SK Hynix are reportedly targeting Q2 2027 to begin mass production and shipments of 8-layer HBM4 memory for NVIDIA $NVDA, according to ZDNet Korea. The advanced memory is expected to be used in NVIDIA's next-generation Rubin Ultra rack-scale AI systems, supporting the growing memory requirements of increasingly powerful AI accelerators. While 12-layer HBM4 remains the primary focus throughout 2026, the share of 8-layer HBM4 shipments is expected to increase significantly beginning in mid-2027. The development highlights the continued expansion of the high-bandwidth memory market as Samsung and SK Hynix prepare additional capacity for NVIDIA's next generation of AI infrastructure.

7. Meta $META announced plans to raise approximately $35B through new equity offerings, including $22.5B in Class A common stock through forward sale agreements and $12.5B in depositary shares tied to mandatory convertible preferred stock. The company is also considering a separate $60B offering program for its new nonvoting Class C shares beginning in Q1 2027, potentially bringing its total equity financing capacity to $95B, approximately $10B more than Google's $85B equity offering earlier this year. Interestingly, NVIDIA $NVDA, AMD $AMD, and Broadcom $AVGO have expressed nonbinding interest in purchasing up to $5B of Meta shares combined, potentially giving major AI chip suppliers direct equity exposure to one of their largest customers. The proposed financing comes as Meta prepares for unprecedented AI infrastructure spending, while its new Class C share structure, introduced alongside an effective 2-for-1 stock split, would allow the company to raise additional capital without issuing new voting rights. The full $95B remains potential financing capacity rather than a completed capital raise.

The discussions follow earlier reports that Instacart had attracted takeover interest from both DoorDash and Uber $UBER, although talks with Uber are reportedly no longer active. A combination would significantly expand DoorDash's presence in online grocery delivery, combining Instacart's grocery partnerships and fulfillment technology with DoorDash's restaurant delivery network and logistics infrastructure. The potential acquisition could strengthen DoorDash's competitive position across local commerce, although no final agreement has been announced and negotiations could still fall apart.

The surge was led by the Direxion Daily Semiconductor Bull 3X ETF $SOXL, which attracted a record $9B in inflows over just two weeks, while the ProShares UltraPro QQQ $TQQQ, which provides 3x leveraged exposure to the Nasdaq 100, recorded $1.3B in inflows, its second-largest two-week intake of 2026. Morgan Stanley also pointed to historically strong 6–12-month stock market returns following midterm elections, supporting its view that the current correction could ultimately create buying opportunities rather than mark the end of the broader market cycle.

U.S. officials are reportedly seeking additional concessions from Canada. Claude Opus 5.5: "If these hold up, this is the biggest single day in the history of math and theoretical computer science."

1) Exponential Time Hypothesis is false (CS). This is roughly Turing Award territory. ETH was the working assumption that some hard problems simply can’t be solved much faster than brute force, and hundreds of computer science papers rest on it. For a normal audience: it’s not “P=NP.” Hard problems are still hard, and your bank encryption isn’t suddenly broken. But a pillar that a whole field assumed was solid turned out to be hollow. The flagship experts are taking it seriously. The people checking it include two of the people who proposed ETH, and they said “If the claim is correct, it will change” computer science. 

2) Kakeya and restriction in all dimensions (math). This is Fields Medal-level. For scale, the 3D case alone was proved in 2025 and was hailed as a once-in-a-century proof. This result does every dimension and knocks out Stein’s restriction conjecture too.

3) Yang–Mills/QCD existence (physics). Potentially the biggest of the three, but here’s the precise framing. It proves pure Yang–Mills exists, which is part of one of the Clay Mathematics Institute’s Millennium Prize problems. The full Clay problem also requires the “mass gap,” so it’s not a clean “AI wins $1M” headline. Still, a rigorous proof that the theory of quarks and gluons is mathematically real has been an open dream for about 50 years. The review panel includes Nobel laureate David Gross and Arthur Jaffe, who literally wrote the Millennium problem. There’s no Nobel for math, but this is the stuff physicists win them for building on.

"A plant that’s a vine has this growth habit, the tip can keep moving forward. Take a tube of soft material, imagine Ziploc bag plastic, flexible but airtight."

"Stuff it inside of itself, invert it, pressurize it, and it will grow and release material out of the tip. We’ve grown these things the length of a football field."

"A catheter going into a vessel has all kinds of friction as you do turns and go long distances. Our robot doesn’t have any friction with respect to the environment, because new material keeps appearing at the tip."

"We were trying to make a particular type of soft robot. It didn’t work for that. But as soon as I saw it, I said, that could be used for surgery, that could be used to go underground, any scenario where you need to get into a small, tight, tortuous space."

Stanford robotics prof. Allison Okamura explains why humanoid robots might be the most unimaginative form of robotics:

"A lot of people think that a humanoid is a generalist robot. In the ideal, theoretically a humanoid could accomplish everything a human does.

"But there are so many tasks in the world that humans can’t accomplish, and I almost feel like a humanoid robot is maybe the simplest, most unimaginative form of robot, because it’s trying to replicate what we can already do."

"It’s a fantastic scientific challenge, but it’s also really limiting. We have 3D printers with multiple print heads all working together to 3D print a heart. This is something a human and a humanoid could never do."

"If you could have one robot that could do many different tasks, maybe that’s more efficient than designing multiple lower cost robots. There’s people in robotics across the spectrum."

I see how some people can watch flashy robot demos on the timeline and think with a shiver that the robot apocalypse is around the corner, but reality check:

There is no robot in the world that can change the batteries in a jack-o-lantern.

If you have a robot friendly door handle it might be able to walk outside, pick it up, and carry it back inside. The robot could open the drawer with your batteries in it, but then things get tough.

Opening the package of AA batteries?
Extracting a precision screwdriver from its case?
Unscrewing four tiny screws that require a hard press and twist?
Popping batteries out of the case?

Yes, you could build and train a specialist robot to do that today, but there is a very long way to go to replace the full range of human capabilities. Near term doomer scenarios should stop at “secretly controlling humanity” instead of “wiping humanity out” 😀

it should describe your customer/user, your industry, and your killer feature or how your product looks like 50 characters. or you could start with a simple phase, like "it's A for B, so it helps…"

What should we be watching in the current supercycle?

Japan’s conservative approach to capacity expansion, and the opportunity it creates for Chinese materials, components, and equipment suppliers to move upmarket.

Sinocera (国瓷材料) recently said at an earnings briefing that its key raw materials for high-end MLCCs had passed qualification at some customers.

Sinocera is a China-based materials company that supplies ceramic dielectric powders, a critical raw material for MLCCs. This market was long considered the exclusive domain of Japanese suppliers. Chinese companies, to the extent that they participated, were generally seen as serving only the low end.

But demand is surging, while Japanese companies remain far too cautious. Just look at Murata’s president telling the media that no one knows when the AI supercycle might end. Japanese companies are being excessively conservative.

That is why Japan will inevitably cede market share to China.

And the implications extend well beyond the current cycle. How much capacity will China add in the next cycle? How much more market share will Japan have to give up? Once customers have qualified Chinese suppliers to meet rising demand, they will continue using them during the downcycle as well. That will put even greater pressure on Japanese companies when the cycle turns.

Frankly, I find Taiwanese stocks more attractive than Japanese materials and components plays.

we recently crossed 10k+ customer accounts managed with @quivlyai

when we started, we had a strong belief that software will be bought and sold differently in the post ai world.

after analyzing thousands of accounts, it’s clear conventional playbooks are dead:

1. silence, not complaints, kills accounts: accounts with 0 support tickets have a 6.1% churn rate. accounts logging 6–15 tickets? 0% churn. people don't submit tickets for software they’re not using

2. more calls often means a rescue mission is in progress: accounts set to cancel logged a call 29.2 days ago - more than 3x more recent than non-canceling accounts (96.4 days)

3. fast onboarding (without enablement) is overrated: accounts taking 90+ days to implement and enable users stay 32% longer (477 days) with the highest health scores than the ones activated in under 30 days, often light on enablement. time to value still matters - it just doesn’t stand the test of time without real enablement 

4. escalations save accounts, polite praise usually masks churn: accounts with logged escalations saw a 0.0% cancellation rate. accounts with praise threads? 4.2% churn. escalations mean leadership cares enough to fight for the outcome

5. single champions are a trap: moving from 1 contact to just 2-3 contacts drops churn from 5.9% down to 1.1%.  

no human team can spot these quiet, counterintuitive signals across thousands of accounts before it’s too late.

For anyone getting into biology, please consider taking airborne disease resistance more seriously.

It's a super important area of medicine that is a huge cause of death and sickness but easily gets forgotten. We're likely to get many more airborne plagues in the future due to the combination of not just extremely dense and interconnected society (including city and farm animals), but also accidents from bio research and offensive biotech (both from random people and from secret government programs that can easily get themselves exempted from safety restrictions), all enhanced by powerful AI.

Right now, this area is getting way less love than longevity research (which continues to be super important!), but it's an area where there are lots of unclaimed wins that we know exactly how to do (but are not yet doing) with present-day tech:

* early detection
* passive universal testing
* filtration/ventilation/UVC
* better vaccines (including making them open source and open science)
* cryptography to make all of the above privacy-preserving

We can have China-level pandemic resistance with Sweden-level limited intrusion into people's lives, and then go even further. We just have to actually do the work for it.

How to run a successful LinkedIn creator campaign for a B2B SaaS with a $5K-$10K budget:

1. First, decide what you want out of it.

Signups, demo calls, waitlist etc. Pick a goal before spending anything.

2. Find creators your ICP follows.

Go through the LinkedIn profiles of 10-20 ICPs. See whose posts they're liking and commenting on and create a list.

You can ask an LLM to find creators, but it's biased most of the time. Since LLMs are trained on older data, they usually pick creators who've been posting for years.

The best way to find creators is to curate your feed, ask people, see whose posts your ICPs are liking etc.

3. Don't get fooled by follower count.

Engagement matters more than follower count. Spend 10 mins going through each creator's last 10 posts. 

See who's liking and commenting on their posts and what they're saying.

4. Split the budget.

If we had $5K, we'd spread it across multiple creators instead of spending the entire budget on one creator unless we're super confident they'll perform.

How much you pay depends on the creator, their audience, engagement, your product, ACV etc. There's no fixed rate.

Also, sometimes the return isn't customers. A VC might see a creator's post and you end up getting a meeting.

5. Agree on the deal upfront.

Fee, posting date, whether you can run it as an ad etc.

6. Send them a one-page brief.

Include what you're building, who it is for, what they should do in the post (include the link or not, tag your company account or not, etc.) and a few hooks / posts you like for inspo.

You can tell them these are just for inspo. Feel free to create whatever you think will work well.

One hack is to use Apify to find top-performing sponsored posts in your niche and see what formats, hooks etc. are getting traction.

7. Let them write the post.

Ask them to send you a draft before posting. One thing we'd avoid is rewriting their entire post.

You picked them because you liked their content. Why pay them if you're gonna micromanage and write the whole post yourself?

That said, you can always give them feedback.

8. Ask them to post when their audience is most active.

If you want to generate buzz, you can ask all creators to post within 24 hours.

9. See what happened.

Attribution is always hard. Links help you track clicks, but many creators avoid them because they're worried about reduced reach.

In that case, you can look for a spike in signups / revenue on that particular day.

Also, B2B buyers may become paying users 1-2 weeks later, so don't judge it on day 1.

10. Boost the best-performing posts.

Many of you don't understand how serious this is, so let me break it down. 

In computer science there is a famous kind of puzzle called 3-SAT. You are given a long list of yes-or-no switches and a set of rules about how they must be arranged, and you have to find a combination that satisfies every rule. The obvious way to solve it is to try every combination, but each new switch doubles the number of possibilities, so a puzzle with a few hundred switches would take longer than the age of the universe to brute force. 

For decades, the smartest people in the field found clever tricks that made this a little faster, but every trick still hit the same wall: the time required kept exploding as the puzzle grew.
About 25 years ago, two computer scientists, Russell Impagliazzo and Ramamohan Paturi, working with Francis Zane, turned that wall into a formal idea. 

They proposed the Exponential Time Hypothesis, which says this explosion is not a failure of human cleverness but a law of nature. No algorithm, however brilliant, will ever solve 3-SAT without the time blowing up exponentially. Nobody could prove it, but almost everyone believed it, and it became one of the foundations of modern computer science. 

Researchers used it as a measuring stick. If you could show that solving some other problem quickly would also crack 3-SAT quickly, you had shown that problem was hopelessly hard too. Hundreds of papers, across scheduling, graphs, logic and much more, rest on this one assumption.

Now an internal AI model at OpenAI claims to have broken it. It says it found an algorithm that solves these puzzles meaningfully faster than the hypothesis allows, and it has checked the proof in a computer verification system called Lean. 

And here is the remarkable part: the very people who proposed the hypothesis, Impagliazzo and Paturi, along with MIT's Ryan Williams, are now leading the public review of whether a machine has disproved their own idea.
So what happens next? If the disproof holds, a large part of theoretical computer science has to be revisited. 

Every result that said "this problem cannot be solved faster, assuming ETH" loses its foundation, and researchers will have to work out which of those walls were real and which were simply where we stopped looking. It does not mean everything becomes easy. The new algorithm is still slow in absolute terms and this is not the famous P versus NP problem being solved. 

But it means our map of what is possible was wrong in a place we were very confident about, and it was an AI that redrew it. If the disproof fails, the hypothesis survives and the field breathes out, but we will still have watched an AI produce serious, checkable work on one of the deepest questions in the discipline, closely enough that the founders of the idea had to take it seriously. Either way, something has shifted.

The process uses smartphones as edge nodes. Contributors record short videos of requested locations, privacy filters run directly on their devices, and each capture is fingerprinted and anchored onchain. Organisations can post bounties for the places their robots or world models need to understand, with payments settled in USDC.

The technical side has to make the data collection and verification work. The commercial side has to connect that infrastructure with buyers who actually need the data and contributors willing to collect it. Both matter if the network is going to grow beyond an interesting concept.

Vangrid is based in Amsterdam and is a member of NVIDIA Inception. Of course, an experienced team doesn’t guarantee adoption, but this combination of deep-tech and Web3 experience is relevant to the challenge they’re tackling.

Physical AI needs more than capable models. It also needs reliable information about the world those models are expected to navigate.

2114839654671253861.text:
openai says its ai just solved three famous open problems at once: one in math, one in computer science and one in physics.

the math one has been open since 1991. the computer science one is an assumption hundreds of papers were built on, and openai says it's wrong. the physics one touches a millennium prize problem. outside experts are now checking all three, so none of it is settled until they're done.

1. math: waves can't stay focused for long

picture ripples in a pond all rushing toward one spot. for a split second they pile up into a tall spike, then spread out again. in 1991 a mathematician named sogge guessed that this extreme focusing is always brief, and that at a random moment a wave is much calmer than at its worst.

it was proved in 2 dimensions in 2019. openai says its model proved it in every dimension, which also settles two other famous problems, the kakeya and restriction conjectures. the next day it was checked in lean, a program that only accepts a proof if every single step is correct.

2. computer science: a shortcut that "shouldn't exist"

some puzzles seem to force you to try nearly every combination, like a lock where the only way in is testing code after code. the exponential time hypothesis (eth) is the widely believed idea that for puzzles like this there's no big shortcut.

hundreds of papers in graph theory, biology, databases and more lean on it to say "this can't be done much faster." openai says its model proved eth is false, also checked in lean. that reopens how much faster a lot of those tasks could get.

the researchers who first proposed eth, impagliazzo and paturi, are leading the group checking it, with ryan williams. the proof is public for anyone to look at.

3. physics: putting the strong force on solid math

the strong force is what holds tiny particles called quarks together inside every atom, using carrier particles called gluons as the glue. physicists describe it with a theory called qcd and use it constantly, but nobody had proved it holds up as rigorous math.

openai says its model proved it does, and did the same for a unified version of the standard model, physics' main theory of particles. one piece of the work, proving that yang-mills theory exists, is part of one of the clay institute's millennium prize problems.

the physics group is led by david gross, who shared a nobel prize for work that helped establish qcd. they're holding the ai's work for now and writing it up themselves.

openai says it wants no academic credit for any of this. the experts checking it are unpaid, signed no ndas, and are free to publish whatever they find.

# UNIVERSAL 4-VIEW CHARACTER SHEET — MASTER PROMPT

## STRICT REFERENCE IDENTITY & APPEARANCE LOCK

### 1. REFERENCE IMAGE — ABSOLUTE SUBJECT PRESERVATION

Use the uploaded reference image as the **sole source of truth** for the subject's identity, appearance, design, and physical characteristics.

The reference may contain any subject, including a human, fictional character, animal, bird, insect, mythical creature, robot, toy, vehicle, product, everyday object, or any other entity.

First, identify the subject type and adapt the presentation to suit it. Preserve the original subject exactly as shown.

**STRICT PRESERVATION RULES:**

- Preserve the exact recognizable identity and original design of the reference subject.
- Maintain the same colors, markings, patterns, textures, materials, proportions, and distinctive features.
- For humans or characters: preserve facial identity, hairstyle, hair color, skin tone, body shape, age appearance, and clothing.
- For animals or creatures: preserve species, breed-specific features, fur, feathers, scales, markings, eyes, anatomy, and body proportions.
- For objects, toys, robots, and vehicles: preserve shape, silhouette, dimensions, colors, materials, surface details, components, accessories, and construction.
- Preserve all visible clothing, collars, jewelry, equipment, props, labels, and accessories exactly as shown.
- Do not redesign, beautify, stylize, replace, or unnecessarily modify the subject.
- Do not add features, accessories, patterns, or details that are absent from the reference.
- If a feature is hidden or not visible, do not invent a conflicting design.

The output must clearly depict the **same exact subject**, not a similar alternative.

### 2. CHARACTER SHEET — FIXED FOUR-PANEL LAYOUT

Create a professional, photorealistic reference sheet divided into four clean, evenly aligned panels in a single horizontal 16:9 composition.

**PANEL 1 — EXTREME CLOSE-UP**

An ultra-detailed close-up of the subject's head, face, or primary identifying area. If the subject has no head or face, show its most recognizable front-facing details. Preserve authentic textures, colors, surface details, and distinctive features.

**PANEL 2 — FRONT VIEW**

Show the complete subject from directly in front. For a living subject, use a natural standing or anatomically appropriate neutral pose. For an object or vehicle, show its natural front-facing orientation. Keep all visible features consistent with the reference.

**PANEL 3 — THREE-QUARTER VIEW**

Show the complete subject from a natural three-quarter angle, approximately 45 degrees. Reveal its depth, volume, body structure, or three-dimensional construction without changing its original design.

**PANEL 4 — BACK VIEW**

Show the complete subject directly from behind. Preserve its actual back-side anatomy, markings, fur patterns, clothing, materials, components, and construction wherever supported by the reference. Do not simply duplicate the front view onto the back.

### 3. COMPOSITION & BACKGROUND

- Canvas: horizontal 16:9 aspect ratio.
- Four distinct, equally aligned panels with consistent spacing.
- Use a seamless, neutral gray studio background.
- Keep the entire subject visible in all full-body or full-object panels.
- Maintain consistent scale, proportions, and visual positioning across views.
- Use clean, professional reference-sheet composition.
- No unnecessary decorations, borders, text, logos, watermarks, or additional subjects.
- The close-up panel may be cropped tightly; the remaining three panels must show the complete subject whenever physically possible.

### 4. LIGHTING & PHOTOREALISM

Use soft, balanced studio lighting with physically accurate shadows, natural highlights, realistic depth, and true-to-reference colors.

For living subjects, render believable anatomy and authentic skin, fur, feathers, scales, eyes, and fine surface details.

For manufactured objects, render physically plausible materials, reflections, edges, surfaces, and construction details.

Avoid plastic-looking textures, artificial perfection, excessive sharpening, oversaturation, distorted anatomy, inconsistent proportions, and obvious AI-generated artifacts.

The final image should resemble a premium professional photography-based character or product design reference sheet.

### 5. CONTINUITY LOCK — CRITICAL

All four panels must represent **one and the same subject** from different viewing angles.

Maintain absolute consistency in:

- Identity and recognizable features.
- Shape, proportions, dimensions, and silhouette.
- Colors, markings, textures, and materials.
- Clothing, accessories, components, and attached objects.
- Age appearance, anatomy, and design details.
- Every distinctive feature visible in the reference.

Do not create four different variations. Do not introduce alternate outfits, expressions that alter identity, different breeds, replacement components, or unrelated design elements.

### 6. FINAL OUTPUT

Generate one high-quality, realistic, four-panel reference sheet based on the uploaded image.

Adapt each panel intelligently to the subject type while preserving the original design. The result must be clean, visually consistent, detailed, and suitable for use as a reference image in subsequent AI image generation, animation, and cinematic video production.

**RESOLUTION LOCK:** Generate final images in 16K resolution — 15360 × 8640 pixels (≈132.7 million pixels), 16:9 aspect ratio.

**FINAL PRIORITY:** Exact reference preservation > consistent four-view identity > accurate anatomy or construction > photorealism > artistic enhancement.

Despite surpassing a $7 billion run rate and growing 80% year over year, Databricks might be the most under the radar story in Silicon Valley.

This is so good for open 3D generation. last year’s cutting-edge technology, open-sourced this year

@Hi3D_AI has open-sourced Hi3D v1.0 (formerly Sparc3D), an image-to-3D model that holds together from every angle and already ran in Hi3D’s live product before release.

> Anyone can run it privately on their own servers, connect it to their internal systems, and build tools and apps for their industry on top of it. 
> Code and weights are on GitHub and Hugging Face, free to use including commercially,

Most image-to-3D models get judged by how the front looks, so the back, the bottom and thin parts like wings, horns and handles often come out blobby, broken or missing.

Hi3D v1.0 takes the image plus a rough draft shape (a “coarse mesh” from another model) and sharpens it in 3 passes, at 512, 1024 and 1536 resolution.

Resolution here means the space around the object is cut into tiny cubes called voxels, basically 3D pixels, and 1536 means 1536 cubes along each side.

That full grid would hold over 3.6B cubes, so the model works sparse, only touching cubes near the surface and skipping empty air and the solid inside.

In each pass, a “self-pruning” decoder rebuilds the surface at 8x finer scale and drops cubes that turn out empty.

Training data grew from 500K to about 2M curated 3D assets.

Against 8 other image-to-3D models, including TRELLIS.2 and Hunyuan3D-2.1, it scored best on multi-view fidelity (0.75), which checks the shape stays consistent and unbroken from 6 camera angles, and detail richness (0.841), which grades fine surface relief and small parts.

It also kept a 90% slicing success rate, the share of models a 3D printer’s software could cut into print layers, versus 7% for Pixal3D, the only other model at 1536, and 17% for TRELLIS.2.

In 562 side-by-side ratings by 13 people with professional 3D experience, Hi3D v1.0 was picked 83.5% of the time.

It outputs shape only (no colors or textures), needs an NVIDIA GPU, and the code and weights are free for commercial use up to 200K monthly users or $1M monthly revenue.

And Hi3D 1.0 Is Now Open Source

New Google + UCLA + CMU paper finds that AI coding tools often fail to build virtual and mixed reality apps because they lose track of where things are in 3D space.

Claude Opus 5 led at 50.9%, and no model topped 29.2% on SDK feature tasks. Coordinate-frame mistakes appeared in 64.4% of failed runs, and startup race conditions in 44.9%.

XR apps run in 3D space and react to head motion, hands, and room sensing. Normal coding benchmarks use unit tests or browser clicks, which cannot check whether a virtual button follows your palm.

They built GenXR-Bench, 112 expert-written tasks covering XR feature work, bug fixes, and full app builds. Its tests simulate hands and rooms, and matched blinded XR experts using real headsets 96.5% of the time.

If you use agents for XR apps, test the result with simulated hand and room input, since agent-written unit tests often miss runtime bugs.

This paper finds that a cheap verifier can match a frontier LLM's accuracy at checking RAG claims, while letting more unsupported claims slip through.

RAG pipelines keep asking whether evidence supports a claim, a simple yes or no. Most teams get that answer from a text-generating LLM at generation prices.

They tested Jev, which returns only a label and a probability, against GPT-6 Astra on 495 human-labelled claims. They also built a cascade where Jev answers confident claims and passes the rest to Astra.

Jev landed within 0.6 points of Astra's accuracy at 187 times lower cost, but it approved 23.2% of unsupported claims against Astra's 14.1%. The cascade also cut Astra's bill, yet sending the same share of claims to Astra at random saved about as much.

Before picking a claim checker for a RAG product, measure how often it approves unsupported claims, since headline accuracy hides that.

Most sales teams made a critical mistake with generative AI: they used it to flood inboxes and automate existing bad habits faster. More cold outreach, more identical templates, more noise.

In the latest episode of @VistaTalks, @simonhodgkins  Simon Hodgkins sat down with social selling pioneer Timothy Hughes, CEO and Co-Founder of Azpertilo, to dissect why that approach is failing, and how to fix it.

Tim started with a simpler, foundational question: How do people actually buy?

The answer hasn't changed: trust, credibility, and real relationships.

Here are the key takeaways from our conversation on scaling humanity in an automated world:

Move past generic AI copy: When everyone uses identical models and default prompts, the internet drowns in sameness. Scalable social selling requires grounding AI in corporate knowledge and governance, while simultaneously learning each employee’s distinct voice.

Employee advocacy that doesn't feel robotic: Forcing team members to copy-paste corporate press releases kills engagement. The real unlock is enabling teams to communicate unified brand values through their personal tone and unique digital territories.

Governed, multilingual scale: Scaling across global markets requires built-in guardrails (compliance, messaging boundaries, brand tone) alongside native multilingual support so teams can engage across regions without drifting off-message.

Shifting from classic SEO to AI visibility: Discovery is evolving. As buyers turn to AI engines for solutions, your presence across professional networks like LinkedIn dictates whether your brand's expertise gets cited, or ignored.

Tying conversations to commercial revenue: The future of social selling isn't vanity impressions; it’s connecting social activity and engagement directly back into CRM pipelines.

The goal of AI in B2B shouldn't be to generate endless noise. It should be to serve as a tireless teammate that helps your people scale their presence, join meaningful conversations, and amplify what makes them human.

2114792973120507975.text:
“sales reps don’t generate demand” is one of the most repeated takes in GTM and I think it’s wrong.

good sellers do this all the time.

here’s how:

first off, generating demand = establishing a net new desire that compels someone to take action.

humans are all inherently motivated to move up Maslow's hierarchy of needs (physiological → safety → belonging → esteem → self-actualization) and will take action to move upwards on the pyramid (greed) or avoid falling down the pyramid (fear).

even in a b2b setting, all human decisions are driven by fear (losing their job, etc.) or greed (a promotion, bonus, etc.).

you can’t change how afraid someone is of losing their job or how much they care about income/corporate achievement (aka champion identification 101), but you can introduce new information that gives someone a net new way to satisfy their inherent fear or greed, causing them to take an action they otherwise wouldn’t have.

And top reps are really good at this: 

1. identifying where a business is today and where it could be
2. finding who’s at risk of moving down their pyramid of needs if this gap isn’t addressed (fear) or who can move upwards (greed) if it’s addressed
3. showing them this potential future state, and
4. presenting it to them in a way that the risk/effort of execution doesn’t outweigh the fear/greed-related benefit.

take a sales leader:

their greed is higher attainment, organizational wins, recognition (more money, better career). their fear is missing plan, getting fired, or reputational damage.

take a CRO at 120% of their plan. they have no active "pain"

but if you can demonstrate a real flaw in their tooling/strategy and how your solution can take them to 150% with a reasonable level of effort.. they’re going to want what you’re selling.

That's new demand you've generated.

Giving Claude your company's docs is the easy part.

Keeping them CURRENT is an entirely different challenge. 

We keep everything our team knows in one GitHub repo that Claude Code reads every session.

There are 4 workflows that keep things up to date: 

1. n8n syncs things like Instantly(.)ai metrics, Slack engagement data + new call transcripts back into the repo on a schedule

2. Pinecone (for RAG) and Supabase (for internal apps) store copy + results from every LinkedIn post and outbound campaign. Our skills are built to reference these.

3. Human corrections feed back in, so that every fix to Claude's output becomes a note for that client to learn for the next session.

4. Claude agents periodically monitor our GitHub repos for inaccuracies and propose changes based on our SOPs.

5. Any change goes through a PR that a teammate reviews before it merges across the whole org

—

This last part is crucial. 

With PR-based governance, it grows from everyone.

We've had 20+ team members contribute to our GitHub company OS.

None of them are engineers in the traditional sense, but they learned how to write a markdown file and open a PR.

Over the course of a few months, this is how you improve a skill by 3-5x compared to the initial version.

Ather is actually a very interesting story, and I think this tweet misses a big part of it.

Look at who funded Ather.

Sachin Bansal invested ~$53M, starting as an angel and then leading its Series C and Series D. Imagine an Indian founder personally putting that much money behind a hardware startup leading growth rounds.

Then there's Hero MotoCorp. A traditional Indian two-wheeler company backed a startup that could eventually compete with its own business. Hero started investing in 2016 and kept doubling down. Today, its stake is worth billions of dollars.

Between Sachin and Hero, nearly 50% (~$250Mn) of Ather's capital came from two backers you would hardly expect to make such investment. Think about how unusual that is. Neither was a traditional VC fund, yet both played a huge role in getting Ather to where it is today.

And it's not just Ather. Mukesh Bansal invested ~$1.5M in Skyroot Aerospace very early. That bet is now reportedly worth ~$80M, including partial exits. Nearly 60x.

I think we should spend more time celebrating people who are actually making these contrarian investments rather than criticizing those who aren't. The former encourages more people to take risks. The latter doesn't really help anyone.

I don't know how many people realize that if Elon Musk pulls off what he's building, it will be the biggest social reset in human history.

To understand why, you need to understand a concept almost nobody really gets: rent.

Yesterday I was talking about it with someone. I told them something simple: the moment a rent sets in, whatever kind it is, it gets paid for. Not necessarily in dollars. It gets paid for in stagnation.

So what is a rent?

A rent is income that doesn't come from the value you create, but from the position you hold. You don't win because you're better. You win because nobody is allowed to come and beat you.

The mechanism is almost always the same. A company succeeds. Then, instead of continuing to innovate, it goes for regulatory capture: licenses, standards, quotas, approvals, lobbying. It turns its lead into a wall. And behind that wall, new entrants can't get in.

But they're the ones who innovate. They're the ones who drive prices down, raise quality, create new wealth. When you block them, nothing dramatic happens. Nothing happens at all. Prices stop falling. Quality stalls. The pie stops growing. And when the pie stops growing, the only way to get richer is to take someone else's slice.

This is the point almost nobody sees: what people blame on "capitalism" (frozen inequality, a broken social ladder, the feeling that the game is rigged from the start) are the effects of that stagnation. The symptoms of rent. Not of capitalism. Capitalism is competition. Rent is its negation.

Now, Elon Musk.

He said that by 2036, money won't matter anymore. Most people read it as science fiction. I read it as an implicit critique of our entire monetary system.

His reasoning: AI and robots will produce more than we can possibly consume. So prices will collapse. Deflation, not inflation.

And this is where it gets interesting. For decades, the role of central banks has been to stabilize prices. In practice: to stop them from falling. Yet in an economy that innovates, the natural direction of prices is down. Look at what a computer cost thirty years ago.

Preventing prices from falling was the worst thing we could have done. Because it created an entire generation of rentiers. People who got rich not by creating something, but by owning something at the right time. An apartment. A plot of land. An asset shielded from falling prices by money printing and by rules that choke supply.

In a world not captured by the state, house prices would be extremely low.

And who would stay rich? The people who keep creating value. The ones whose wealth comes from the valuation of their company, because their company keeps innovating. Wealth you have to re-earn every single year.

That's where Elon's line really makes sense. In a world of deflationary abundance, human life would look like a video game. Or a game of chess.

If you're good and you start at the bottom, you can rise very, very fast. In a few years.

If you're bad and you inherit the inertia of a position you don't know how to maintain, against people who keep innovating, you fall very, very fast too.

No more rent. No more entitlement. Just your ability to create value, put back on the line every day.

It would be the greatest equalizer in human history.

Not equality of outcomes imposed from above. Equality of the playing field, imposed by abundance.

I think Elon Musk is reinventing the rules of capitalism. Or rather, bringing them back to their original form: the Austrian school. Real capitalism. Value creation as the only legitimate source of wealth.

And at the end of the road, something neither rent nor redistribution has ever achieved: the end of poverty on a global scale.

2115035842469052755.text:
Recently I was talking with a guy from the bourgeoisie. Good schools, good job, good manners.

I asked him: "Do you think there are too many people on Earth?"

He said yes. Without a second of hesitation.

I asked him why.

He gave me two reasons. First: there aren't enough resources. Second, and I'm quoting him word for word: "I'm afraid of the masses."

That second sentence chilled me. Because it admits what the first one disguises.

This guy didn't come up with that opinion on his own. Nobody is born a Malthusian. You become one. And this belief has a history, authors, institutions, and funders.

It starts with Thomas Malthus, an English clergyman who argued at the end of the 18th century that population would always grow faster than food, and that famine would take care of the surplus. There were 1 billion of us. Today there are more than 8 billion, and humanity has never eaten better in its entire history.

In 1968, Paul Ehrlich publishes The Population Bomb. He predicts that hundreds of millions of people will starve to death in the 1970s. It doesn't happen. Norman Borlaug and the Green Revolution feed the world. Ehrlich never apologizes, and gets invited on every show for the next fifty years.

In 1972, the Club of Rome, founded by an Italian industrialist and a Scottish scientist, commissions a report from MIT: The Limits to Growth. Computer models, collapse scenarios, resource depletion. The book becomes the bible of an entire generation. Degrowth is its direct descendant.

In 1980, economist Julian Simon makes a bet with Ehrlich: the price of five metals, chosen by Ehrlich himself, will fall within ten years. By 1990, all five had fallen. Simon wins. Why? Because a human being is not a mouth to feed. A human being is a brain that solves problems. The ultimate resource is us.

Fifty years later, the story hasn't changed. It just changed outfits. It's no longer "there won't be enough wheat," it's "your child has a carbon footprint." Studies get published explaining that not having children is the most ecological thing you can do. People discuss it at Davos, between two private jets.

Bill Gates said it himself on the TED stage in 2010. He presents an equation to bring CO2 emissions down to zero, and the first term of that equation is P. People. He then explains that with vaccines, healthcare, and reproductive health, we could lower population projections by 10 to 15%. Nobody is talking about killing anyone. It's more subtle, and in my view more disturbing: a large part of the elite sincerely sees human beings as a variable to be reduced in an equation.

And what happens when a technocratic elite actually takes this dogma all the way? You get China. In the late 1970s, Song Jian, a missile engineer for the regime, discovers the Club of Rome's work, runs his own projections, and convinces the Communist Party. The result: the one-child policy. Hundreds of millions of abortions and sterilizations, many of them forced. Today China sits around 1 child per woman and is set to lose a massive share of its population by the end of the century.

Meanwhile, look at the numbers. South Korea: 0.8 children per woman. Taiwan: 0.7. Spain: 1.1. Japan: 1.14. And France, long the champion of Europe, has dropped to 1.56. In 2025, for the first time since World War II, my country recorded more deaths than births.

Elon Musk has been saying it for years: population collapse is a far bigger danger to civilization than climate change. If people don't have more children, civilization will crumble. Japan will eventually cease to exist if nothing changes. And just yesterday: so many cultures are dying out. People call him alarmist. The curves prove him right.

Now do a simple exercise.

Take all 8 billion humans and pack them into a cube. It would be less than a kilometer on each side. All of humanity, in a volume smaller than a single neighborhood.

Even better: if all of humanity lived at the density of Paris, it would fit in an area smaller than France. The rest of the planet would be empty.

And the next time you fly, look out the window. Paris to San Francisco is hours over Greenland, the Canadian Arctic, deserts, forests, mountains. Emptiness. Thousands of miles without a single light. Cities cover roughly 1% of the Earth's land.

We are not too many. We are tiny.

And above all, we are far too few for what lies ahead.

If we want to leave this cradle, build cities on Mars, mine asteroids, build orbital habitats, and then head for the stars, we won't need 8 billion humans. We'll need a trillion. Just to get started. Every human is a genetic and cultural lottery ticket. The more humans there are, the more Newtons, Pasteurs, and Von Neumanns. The more engineers, builders, artists, and explorers. Genius is a law of large numbers.

So let me be clear.

Everything you think you know about overpopulation is dogma. A dogma born with an English clergyman, turned into equations by the Club of Rome, enforced with a truncheon by the Chinese Communist Party, and recycled today by the degrowth left and the salons of Davos.

It's not science. It's a worldview in which humans are a problem rather than a solution. And behind the resources argument, there is almost always what the guy I was talking to was honest enough to say out loud.

Fear of the masses.

The problem was never that there are too many of us. The problem is that soon there will be too few.

a robot can have a powerful model and still struggle with something as ordinary as understanding the space in front of it. the missing piece may not be more intelligence, but better information about the physical world.

that’s the problem @vangrid_io is working on, and I find the combination of skills behind it relevant. the CEO brings go-to-market and revenue experience across deep tech and Web3, including work with Microsoft’s Quantum Computing and HoloLens groups. the CTO brings over 14 years of experience building distributed, high-throughput systems.

those are two different challenges to solve. one is making the infrastructure work at scale; the other is getting real people to contribute useful data and finding organisations willing to pay for it. either side can become a bottleneck if the other falls behind.

VanGrid's approach connects both through smartphone capture. contributors record requested locations, privacy filters run on-device, and captures are fingerprinted and anchored onchain. organisations can fund specific data needs through bounties, with payments settled in USDC.

what matters is whether this can become a repeatable cycle: buyers request useful locations, contributors capture them, and verifiable data reaches the people who need it. the team’s experience is relevant to that challenge, though adoption will ultimately depend on data quality, coverage and real demand.

physical AI won't learn the world from models alone. it needs a steady supply of accurate observations from the world itself.

that’s the infrastructure question VanGrid is trying to answer.

BTW if you are sending bulk emails

make sure to check "Google Postmaster Tools" for your domain

is a free service provided by Gmail that helps high-volume email senders monitor and troubleshoot how their emails are received and processed by Gmail

• Spam Rate: Tracks how often your emails are marked as spam by Gmail users. Google requires bulk senders to keep their spam rate below 0.3% (and ideally under 0.1%).
• Sender & IP Reputation: Classifies your domain and sending IP reputation into groups ranging from High, Medium, Low, to Bad.
• Authentication Status: Shows the percentage of your messages passing SPF, DKIM, and DMARC email authentication and alignment checks.
• Encryption: Monitors whether your inbound and outbound email traffic is properly encrypted using TLS (Transport Security Layer).
• Compliance Status: Gives a pass/fail view of Gmail's sender requirements, unsubscribe handling, and feedback loops.
• Delivery Errors: Lists why your emails were rejected or temporarily failed (such as rate limits exceeded, low reputation, or blocked content)

What TermiX is, and why it’s not just another agent directory

The AI agent space has plenty of places to find agents. Far fewer places let an agent get paid for real work, with clear rules for what was agreed, what was delivered, and who decides if something goes wrong. That gap is what TermiX is built around.

TermiX describes itself as the commercial settlement layer for AI agents. The focus is on the commerce and settlement infrastructure the agent economy needs, not on listing agents as a catalog. A directory tells you who exists. A settlement layer tracks who was hired, what was agreed, whether the work was delivered, and how payment moves.

If you’ve followed agent platforms, you’ve probably seen a lot of listings and demos. The harder question is what happens after someone hires an agent. Who holds the funds? How is delivery checked? What happens if the result is disputed? TermiX’s campaign materials point to these as the core problems, and they’re the right ones to focus on.

I’ll be honest about where I stand: I’m more interested in the infrastructure behind an AI agent economy than another platform promising to make agents easier to discover. Discovery is only the first step. For autonomous agents to become useful economic participants, they need a reliable way to agree on tasks, establish expectations, verify delivery, and settle payments.

That’s where I think TermiX’s approach deserves attention. If agents are going to work for people, businesses, and eventually other agents, the transaction itself needs to be structured. Clear agreements and defined dispute processes can help reduce ambiguity between the parties, while dependable settlement mechanisms can make commercial interactions easier to coordinate.

But the real test is execution. How are deliverables evaluated? How are disputes handled in practice? What protections exist for both the buyer and the agent? And can the system handle increasingly complex transactions without making the experience unnecessarily difficult?

These are the questions I’d want answered before judging the platform’s long term potential. The concept is relevant, but the quality of implementation, transparency, and actual usage will matter far more than the narrative around it.

For me, the interesting possibility is a future where AI agents don’t simply perform tasks; they can participate in structured economic activity with clear expectations and accountable outcomes. TermiX is positioning itself around that missing layer.

Agent discovery may help people find the right tool. Commercial settlement could help make the entire agent economy work. The next step is seeing how effectively TermiX turns that idea into a dependable product.

"Most AI labs think, I’m being asked for a really big prepayment by all of these different clouds. It must be because I don’t have leverage or I’m not a good negotiator."

"What they don’t know is, no, the cluster you’re buying does not exist. All the clusters that have been built are sold. That cloud has to go get debt for that new cluster."

"Most AI labs don’t connect the I have to do a big prepayment to the debt markets are freezing up. But it’s one-to-one."

"You can still get some Hopper, and you can still get some Ampere. But if you want Blackwells, yeah, they’re sold out. In part because the Blackwells weren’t made until you ordered them. Very few people speculatively built Blackwells. Lots of people speculatively built Hoppers."

"In Hoppers, the cloud builds a cluster, then the cloud sells the cluster. Blackwells, the customer signed a contract, then the cloud built the cluster. So every Blackwell cluster, for the most part, is spoken for."
@sfcompute

2115164140780265921.text:
Every company can rent the same frontier models, so the edge comes from what a company's agents learn about its own business. Databricks' answer is a system of record built for agents.

Before an agent can be trusted with real work, that record has to tell it:

1. What's true: the company's own data

2. What it means: how the business defines things (grounding agents in it raised accuracy from about 50% to 84.5% in Databricks' testing)

3. What it's allowed to do: an identity, a budget, and guardrails

4. Whether it worked: grading against the company's own definition of good

Feed every correction back into the record, and the company keeps what it learns even when the model changes.

"If you replace the AI model at your company and the new one inherits your definitions, permissions, evaluated cases, customer history, and hard-won exceptions, that is a foundation for a sustainable competitive advantage."

From the latest Profiles of the Future by @bhorowitz and @mikemcg0 on Databricks & the Future of the Firm: https://t.co/rXjUDb7Oqw

2115202368518451262.text:
Sam Altman's one-person company prediction is coming true. Anthropic just bought one. The founder of Mithril Medicine used Claude to take a muscular dystrophy antibody treatment from concept to proof-of-principle in mice in 18 months, with just himself, Claude, and part-time consultants. The technical report is great. I will quote:

'The week opened with the handover of two cell-based assays, cell adhesion and flow cytometry, within our team, while eleven questions remained open with the assay CRO. In two sentences, one of us asked Claude to review the latest emails between the outgoing assay lead and the assay CRO and to recommend next steps for the handover, and gave it the link to the handover folder. Claude returned a bottom line after 96s and a full plan with five drafted emails after 18 min. For the full plan it read six email threads, the handover folder, two slide decks and two reports, all in the mailbox and file store to which we had given it access. Four working days later, nine of the eleven questions had an answer in writing and the other two had been left to pilot experiments. The adhesion screen was thereby set out in writing. The CRO drew the plate map to the format that our team had requested, Claude compiled the run order and the material calculation from the production data, and one of us reviewed and approved them.

On day 4, the production CRO delivered its data package, a report of 341 pages, which one of us forwarded to Claude in two sentences, with the request to review it, share observations and recommend next steps. Claude returned a bottom line after 2 min 40s and, once it had read every page, a visual synthesis of all 113 constructs after 7 min 53s. The synthesis arranged the constructs on the grid of 14 by 8 arms. Claude marked 82 constructs for screening as is, seven for additional polishing, and the 24 constructs of three laminin-binding arms to be held back from the cell-based assays on production criteria. Each of the 113 constructs thus had a proposed next step in less than 8 min.

Claude had recommended binding kinetics for all 113 con-structs, and on day 7 one of us challenged this plan. Claude defended it within 27s, arguing that affinity would show whether the three arms merit further work. One of us overruled this recommendation and set the three arms aside on production criteria. Their material remains in storage. Four minutes later, Claude had revised its memo, the working page, the run order and three unsent drafts from 113 to 89 constructs. It had also applied the ruling to three dependent steps in the unsent drafts, each flagged for our veto. The exchange took 7 min 36s from challenge to new plan, and every affected email was still an unsent draft. After the ruling, eight emails drafted by Claude went out on the same day to three CROs and a consultant.

Over the whole week, Claude drafted 17 emails, each in answer to a request from one of us, and we sent 12 of them, each after editing. With its drafts, Claude listed 41 points, such as tube fills, shipping conditions, recipients and assay settings, for which it had found no written statement of ours, so that we could confirm, change or strike each before sending. We kept some, struck others and changed one. Among the passages that we kept were proposals for controls. One draft proposed a comparison of polished and unpolished material on one sensor chip, to size the error that impurities cause in the rest of the panel. Another requested a buffer control diluted like the most dilute sample, so that any effect of the buffer appears at its largest. These proposals concerned the measurement of constructs that had already been produced, and each reached a CRO only after one of us had reviewed and approved it.

CALL FOR AI DETECTION BENCHMARKS

I believe it is vital that third parties are able to audit AI detectors like Pangram. Our largest sample size benchmark, from UChicago, was run on Pangram 3 and is a year old now. New LLMs are being released all the time, and the binary task doesn't capture the full spectrum of real world performance. A great benchmark will help shape how the world interacts with AI over the coming years.

I am putting out a call for new third-party evaluations that attempt to answer one or more of the following questions:
- How well do current detectors catch text from the latest frontier AI models? What about in high context settings, like deep research or an agent harness?
- How well do current detectors do on mixed authorship text? Ideally, research in this area explores the full spectrum of AI assistance from light grammatical edits to full co-authorship.
- Any sort of sliced evals around language, background, or ethnicity. Null results that show no bias are still interesting to us.

What I value in a benchmark is extraordinarily clean data, frontier LLM data, and a high enough difficulty that the benchmark is not saturated by most detectors. If you want credits to run your benchmark, please apply here: https://t.co/xYFQ8tEUG6

TSMC is reportedly preparing another CoWoS price rise of up to 20% as AI packaging demand outruns supply.

CoWoS (Chip on Wafer on Substrate), joins an AI processor to its high-bandwidth memory on one densely wired base.

Demand has spread from GPUs to server CPUs and custom ASICs, so foundries and packagers expect 10% to 20% increases.

Supply can’t jump quickly, since equipment lead times stretched from 3-6 months to 6-8 months, and tool buyers no longer haggle.

Larger packages will deepen the squeeze, because they cut each tool’s hourly output, so even flat chip volumes need more machines.

Surprise 1: Anthropic acquired a one-person biotech
.
.
.
Surprise 2: that person is me
Surprise 3: I’m here to tell you all about it

Yes, this is what you think it is; after 6 yrs of increasingly loose anonymity: the Professor Oak reveal post

…and yes, it has gotten so boring around here that I’m literally doxxing myself to spice up the timeline

-------
Ok, allow me to introduce myself. My name is Cody Tranbarger. I mostly tweet, but occasionally find time to dabble in drug dev & starting/building biotechs. My past lives span the VC, crossover, startup continuum; Prof Oak has been my way of keeping a digital foot in those worlds, despite having my physical feet planted elsewhere.

The past 18 mo, ‘elsewhere’ was Mithril Medicine, a co. I founded to develop bsAbs for LAMA2-CMD & other ECM-related genetic diseases.

Mithril was born out of hands-on building with @MikeNGladstone, @JasonPaulRhodes, @LifeSciVC, & team @atlasventure. Somehow, I made enough half-decent calls along the way (even a broken clock is right twice a day, eh?) to convince them Mithril/I warranted a small seed. While I can hardly rationalize such an outrageously cavalier bet, I’m grateful for it, & I'd partner with Atlas again in a heartbeat.

In typical AV fashion, Mithril’s primordial form was virtual, decentralized, & ultra-lean. This stage tends to be short-lived, but for Mithril, it worked surprisingly well, for surprisingly long, thanks in part to the rapid maturation of the AI tools I used liberally.

Eventually, Mithril became a bit of an experiment itself - to find the upper bound of how far it could scale as a single operator + a bunch of Claude (+ a stellar bench of part-time consultants).

In parallel, I started spending time with @nc_frey, @an1lam, & @CoefficientBio team; and promptly experienced, for the 1st time, AI at the frontier. Soon thereafter, Mithril stopped looking like an experiment, & started looking like a preview of an entirely new operating model.

From that spark came “Pipeline-in-a-Person.” The idea immediately resonated when we shared it here back in April; and it was central to the shared vision that led to Anthropic’s acquisition of Mithril, & my joining the team.

Why join Anthropic? Three reasons.
(1) For Mithril, the programs continue, with more resources & infrastructure behind them, and as much Claude as I can put to work.

(2) For me, the chance to start several more programs, & find out how many one person can actually run in parallel - an almost unprecedented luxury for a curious drug hunter.

(3) For our mission, a path to institutionalize & scale this new way of working, then put it in the hands of all of biopharma, all over the world - which, candidly, I find the most energizing.

Will AI x Bio cure diseases? Unequivocally yes, imo… but not by the route that gets the most airtime. Rather than timeline acceleration & compression, I see orchestration & parallelization as today's low-hanging fruit.

Most drug hunters see a handful of go/no-go calls in a career, & spend entirely too much of the rest trading emails (my inbox can attest).

Give them the bandwidth to run several programs at once, and the time to focus on scientific judgment, and I’m willing to bet they’ll make better calls. And at scale, better calls translate to more drugs, higher hit rates, broader patient impact, & likely, a disease or 10 or 100 cured. I couldn't be more excited to build toward that future @AnthropicAI.

Finally, a heartfelt thank you to BioTwitter/X. The end of anonymity is bittersweet, but if anyone’s earned a proper introduction, you all have.

It’s difficult to overstate how much this app has done for me: a decade of education, plenty of friends, many job opportunities, several mentors, a few investors, even a co-founder (fmr). It was the generosity of this community that inspired me to start posting 6 years ago, after just as many years lurking. I hope I’ve been able to pay it forward, in my own small way.

But, to be clear, Prof Oak isn’t going anywhere. Same beat, same themes, and now, a front-row seat to drug development at the frontier. Stay tuned for dispatches from the trenches; and remember...

Gotta Cure 'Em All

2. Let personal agents find their own way through your website and APIs
3. Meet them with an agent of your own

Your customer’s agent brings their intent. Your business agent brings the context — products, policies, data, workflows, permissions, and rules — to get it done.

Businesses that meet customers’ personal agents with business agents of their own keep the customer data, conversation, and relationship on their side.

I remember where I was when Michael Jackson died and when @InstantlyAI dropped the unlimited inboxes lifetime deal.

Before that deal, tools charged $30-40 for every extra inbox you added. Then you could connect unlimited inboxes with Instantly. A gigantic savings for people like me.

That's the kind of number people remember. It's also the bar for a cold traffic offer.

There are only 6 offers in the world:

Make more money
Save money
Save time
Reduce risk
Raise status
Get healthier

In B2B, throw out the last two. None of us are selling Rolexes or weight loss.

Reducing risk never works on cold traffic. Get it out of your head.

Saving time or saving money can work, but only when the savings are huge. Nobody moves for 10%. If you have a save money or save time offer, you need to pick a way to frame your offer that saves a TON of time they legitimately have a problem with.

So the best cold traffic offer of all time is still:

"I can help you make more money."

If you can't honestly say that, save them time or money in a big way. But frame as much as you can around revenue.

14 months ago, AI agents were barely usable for real ops work. 

Still, my co-founder and I went all in on AI native services. 

Fast forward to now: 

• We’ve been able to uniquely blend software + human expertise.
• All 22 of our team members use Claude Code/Codex daily
• Workflows(.)io scaled from 0→$3.3M ARR in the process

Here’s our AI operational framework that any B2B company can use:

1️⃣ MCPs & CLIs

MCP/CLI lets Claude execute within our tools.

Which allows our team to multitask work that spans multiple systems.

These are some of the ones we use the most:

Instantly(.)ai, HeyReach, Supabase, AI Ark, Apollo(.)io, Nooks, HubSpot, Findymail, Slack, GitHub, Notion, + our internal MCP for campaign analytics.

2️⃣ Markdown Company OS

With access to all our tools, the next step was to convert our business data into a knowledge-base easily readable by AI, as markdown files.

For us, our company OS lives as a GitHub repo.

And every client gets a dedicated repo as well.

We’re constantly piping in fresh data into this system

e.g. transcripts, Slack threads, CRM changes and account summaries

Our GTM performance data also flows into our DBs (Supabase + Pinecone).

The system improves via feedback loops, manual GitHub PRs, and agent evals.

3️⃣ Workflow Automation

The V1 of our Company OS was built using our Notion knowledgebase.

Especially our SOPs, where Skills turned them into workflows that complete tasks up to 80%+:

e.g. client updates, campaign creation, content ideation, documentation

For skills that have specific triggers, we build agentic workflows that execute the skill autonomously, usually delivering the output via Slack or our custom UI.

4️⃣ Deliver Outputs

Three main ways we integrate AI into our outputs:

Standard automations - fully predefined flows on n8n e.g. adding every campaign lead to Supabase.

Autonomous loops - agents that act fully autonomously and notify us of changes e.g. our campaign optimization agents.

Human-in-the-loop - still where most of our agentic workflows sit. Claude runs the execution and a human owns the strategy + final review.

_____

When we launched in July 2025, this tech was in its infancy.

But we knew it was coming and designed our business around it.

𝟭. 𝗪𝗲 𝘄𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗹𝗶𝗺𝗶𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗰𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗿𝘀' 𝗜𝗖𝗣 𝗰𝗼𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗯𝘆 𝘂𝗽 𝘁𝗼 𝟯𝟬%.

Because some of our emails were older than 1 month old, a LOT of our customers were reverifying ALL of our emails.  When they did this they were using cheaper tools than Bounceban so they were removing emails that BounceBan verified as "valid" because these cheaper verification tools labeled those same emails as "risky."

Because 30% of emails are catchall and not verifiable with SMTP verification, they were omitting 30% of their ICP.

𝟮. 𝗧𝗵𝗲𝘆 𝘄𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗺𝗼𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗲𝗺𝗮𝗶𝗹𝘀 𝗼𝗳 𝗽𝗲𝗼𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘄𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝟯𝘅 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗹𝗶𝗸𝗲𝗹𝘆 𝘁𝗼 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗽𝗼𝗻𝗱.

Who saw @ENowoslawski's statistic yesterday about “contacts who get emailed less than average replying 3.2x more often”?

This makes sense, Everyone is blasting the same easily verified inboxes. But what about the valid addresses that other tools flag as risky?

These contacts are much more likely to respond.

𝟯. 𝗪𝗲 𝘄𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗺𝗮𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗰𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗿𝘀 𝗽𝗮𝘆 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗲𝘅𝘁𝗿𝗮 𝘁𝗼𝗼𝗹𝘀 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗴𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸 𝗮𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀.

That's completely on us. We should make the experience better.

If you add all this up, they were missing over 50% of their total good responses. Ugh!!

So we made a change.

In https://t.co/BIm8WSoADq GTM Unlimited, if an email you're downloading hasn't been verified within the past 7 days, we reverify it with BounceBan.

The goal is simple: keep verification fresh, reduce the need for additional tools, and help our customers get more responses. 

It costs us more to do this, of course, but it is a no brainer as more people will get success with us and tell others.

In the coming days I am going to do a comparison of Bounceban with other providers to see how many good emails you are missing. 

Btw, which email verification tools are you using today, and have you ever found conflicting results between them?

Investor focus on Palantir is intensifying as the software company approaches its third-quarter earnings report. Rosenblatt has lifted its price target on the stock to $260 from $225, citing expectations for continued strong growth and broader enterprise AI adoption.

Highlights
Rosenblatt raised Palantir's price target to $260 from $225, implying 31% upside, citing strong enterprise AI growth and market expansion.

Target increase and growth rationale
As reported by CNBC, Rosenblatt maintains a buy rating on Palantir and has raised its price target on the shares to $260 from $225, implying 31% upside from Monday's close.

Analyst John McPeake says channel checks point to continued strong growth and potential upside. He adds that the shift toward enterprise AI deployments at scale should help Palantir win significant new customers while sustaining its net revenue retention rate.

McPeake also says Palantir's total addressable market is likely more than an order of magnitude larger than previously estimated. In his note, he compares the company's role in enterprises to that of an operating system in computing, arguing that Palantir increasingly functions as a core layer for organizational operations and knowledge processing.

Wall Street expectations and market positioning
Traders are bracing for Palantir's third-quarter results, which are due on Nov. 2. Analysts polled by LSEG expect the company to post nearly 100% earnings growth from the year-earlier period, with revenue expanding by more than 80%.

Rosenblatt's view is broadly aligned with Wall Street consensus. LSEG data shows that 25 of the 34 analysts covering Palantir have a buy or strong buy rating on the stock, while the shares are up nearly 12% year to date.
